learn: Our solar system has one star, the Sun, and eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The four inner planets are small and rocky. The four outer planets are giant worlds made mostly of gas and ice.
The solar system also holds dwarf planets like Pluto, moons, asteroids and comets.
check: How many planets are in our solar system?
lessons.try: Make a scale model of planet distances using a long strip of paper.

learn: Gravity is a force of attraction between all objects that have mass.
The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull. The farther apart objects are, the weaker the pull.
The Sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit. Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in orbit.
check: Gravity gets weaker when objects are...
What keeps planets orbiting the Sun?
lessons.try: Swing a ball on a string in a circle and explain how the string acts like gravity.

learn: Space distances are huge. Scientists use the astronomical unit (AU), the average Earth-Sun distance of about 150 million km.
Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
check: One AU is the distance from...
Neptune is about ___ AU from the Sun.
lessons.try: Calculate how many times farther Neptune is from the Sun than Earth.

units.t: Earth, Moon and Sun: Seasons, Phases and Eclipses

learn: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees.
As Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere takes turns tilting toward the Sun, getting more direct light and longer days: summer.
Seasons are not caused by distance from the Sun. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
check: When it is summer in the north, the south has...
lessons.try: Use a lamp and a tilted ball to show summer in each hemisphere.

learn: The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight.
As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half: new, crescent, quarter, gibbous and full.
A full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.
check: A full cycle of phases takes about...
When we see none of the lit side, it is a...
lessons.try: Draw the Moon every night for two weeks and label each phase.

learn: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight.
A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, casting a shadow on the Moon.
Never look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse; use certified eclipse glasses or a pinhole viewer.
check: In a solar eclipse, what is in the middle?
In a lunar eclipse, what casts the shadow?
Safe ways to view a solar eclipse include...
lessons.try: Use a lamp, ball and marble to model both kinds of eclipse.

learn: A star is a huge ball of hot gas that makes its own light and heat.
Stars differ in size, colour and brightness. Blue stars are hottest; red stars are coolest.
The Sun is a medium-sized yellow star.
lessons.try: Look at a star chart and find a red star and a blue star.

learn: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.
Medium stars like the Sun swell into red giants and end as white dwarfs.
Very massive stars can end in a supernova explosion, leaving a neutron star or black hole.
check: Very massive stars can end in a...
lessons.try: Draw a flowchart of a star's life cycle.

learn: A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars.
Distances between stars are measured in light-years: the distance light travels in one year.
check: The Milky Way is a ___ galaxy.
lessons.try: On a dark night, look for the band of the Milky Way.

units.t: Minerals, Rocks and the Rock Cycle

learn: A mineral is a naturally formed, non-living solid with a crystal structure.
Geologists identify minerals by colour, streak, lustre, hardness and cleavage.
The Mohs scale rates hardness from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
check: The softest mineral on the Mohs scale is...
The colour of a mineral's powder is its...
lessons.try: Test which of your rock samples can be scratched by a fingernail or a coin.

learn: Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens: granite, basalt.
Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment are pressed and cemented: sandstone, limestone.
Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change existing rock: marble, slate.
lessons.try: Sort a rock collection into the three kinds.

learn: The rock cycle shows how rocks change from one kind to another over long periods.
Weathering, erosion, melting, cooling, heat and pressure drive the cycle.
Any type of rock can become any other type.
lessons.try: Draw the rock cycle with arrows labelled by process.

learn: Earth has a crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
The crust and upper mantle are broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates.
Plates move a few centimetres a year, slowly floating on the hot mantle below.
check: The thin outer layer of Earth is the...
The centre of Earth is the...
lessons.try: Label a diagram of Earth's layers.

learn: At divergent boundaries plates move apart, forming ridges and rift valleys.
At convergent boundaries plates push together, forming mountains or trenches.
At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, like the San Andreas Fault.
check: Plates moving apart is a ___ boundary.
The Himalayas formed at a ___ boundary.
The San Andreas Fault is a ___ boundary.
lessons.try: Use two pieces of foam to model each boundary type.

learn: Earthquakes happen when rocks along a fault suddenly slip, sending out seismic waves.
Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, often at plate boundaries or hot spots like Hawaii.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur around the Pacific "Ring of Fire".
check: The area around the Pacific with many quakes is the...
lessons.try: Mark recent earthquakes on a world map and look for patterns.

learn: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces.
Mechanical weathering breaks rock physically: ice wedging, roots and rubbing.
Chemical weathering changes what rock is made of, as when acidic rain dissolves limestone.
check: Ice in cracks widening rock is...
lessons.try: Find examples of weathering on buildings, pavements or gravestones.

learn: Erosion moves weathered material by water, wind, ice and gravity.
Deposition drops material in a new place, building deltas, beaches and sand dunes.
Rivers carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.
check: Erosion is the ___ of weathered material.
The Grand Canyon was carved mainly by...
lessons.try: Build a sand slope and pour water to watch erosion.

learn: Fossils are preserved remains or traces of ancient living things, usually found in sedimentary rock.
The law of superposition says lower rock layers are usually older than layers above.
Fossils and layers help scientists build Earth's history, which is about 4.6 billion years old.
lessons.try: Make a layered model with different colours of clay and "fossils".

units.t: The Water Cycle and Earth’s Water

learn: The Sun's energy drives the water cycle.
Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects as runoff and groundwater.
Plants also release water vapour through transpiration.
lessons.try: Make a mini water cycle in a sealed bag taped to a sunny window.

learn: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
Most fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice caps; only a small part is easy to use.
Groundwater fills spaces in rock underground in layers called aquifers.
lessons.try: Use 100 cups of water to model how much is fresh and usable.

learn: Ocean currents move huge amounts of water around the world.
Surface currents are driven by wind; deep currents by differences in temperature and saltiness.
Currents carry heat and affect climate, like the Gulf Stream warming western Europe.
check: Surface currents are driven mostly by...
lessons.try: Trace the Gulf Stream on a world map.

learn: The atmosphere is a layer of gases around Earth, mostly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%).
Weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere.
The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet light.
lessons.try: Draw the layers of the atmosphere.

learn: Air masses are large bodies of air with similar temperature and humidity.
A front is the boundary where two air masses meet.
Cold fronts often bring quick storms; warm fronts bring steady rain.
check: The boundary between air masses is a...
lessons.try: Read a weather map and find a cold front and a warm front.

learn: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place and time.
Climate is the average weather pattern over many years.
Latitude, altitude, oceans and mountains all affect climate.
check: Places near the equator are usually...
lessons.try: Compare the climate of your town with a town near the equator.

learn: Renewable resources can be replaced naturally: sunlight, wind, water and trees.
Nonrenewable resources take millions of years to form: coal, oil and natural gas.
Using resources wisely helps them last.
lessons.try: Sort a list of resources into renewable and nonrenewable.

learn: Air pollution comes from vehicles, factories and burning fuels.
Water pollution includes litter, chemicals and runoff from farms and streets.
Pollution harms living things and people's health.
check: A source of air pollution is...
lessons.try: Do a litter survey of your school grounds.

learn: Conservation means protecting and using resources carefully.
Reduce, reuse and recycle cut waste.
Engineers design solutions like solar panels, wind turbines and water filters.
check: The first of the three Rs is...
lessons.try: Make a plan to reduce waste at home for a week.

learn: Natural hazards include earthquakes, volcanoes, floods, hurricanes, tornadoes and wildfires.
Some hazards are linked to weather; others to movements inside Earth.
Scientists study patterns to know where hazards are likely.
lessons.try: Find which natural hazards are most common where you live.

learn: Weather satellites and radar track storms.
Seismometers measure earthquakes.
Warning systems give people time to get to safety.
lessons.try: Learn what a "watch" and a "warning" mean for storms.

learn: Make a family emergency plan with meeting places and contacts.
Keep an emergency kit with water, food, a torch, batteries and a first-aid kit.
In an earthquake: drop, cover and hold on.
check: Stand in a doorway on the stairs
lessons.try: Make a checklist for a family emergency kit.
